12997-the-pony-rider-boys-in-the-grand-c:
Frank Gee Patchin's Pony Rider Boys in the Grand Canyon, subtitled The Mystery of Bright Angel Gulch, sends Tad Butler and his friends westward to the canyon rim. Tad chops wood at home, deaf to yells behind him until his stick is finished, then turns smiling to adventure. A night in a crater, a city in the skies, and a roaring Colorado follow.

A trail scene shows the danger: ponies pick over rocks and sharp corners, where one misstep sends horse and rider crashing hundreds of feet down. Stacy jokes about borrowing an Indian basket to carry a fallen friend home. The book offers lively canyon adventure for young readers.
14479-narrative-of-services-in-the-liber:
Thomas, Earl of Dundonald, the Scots naval hero, wrote this second volume of his liberation memoirs in 1859, covering his service to Brazil after earlier campaigns in Chile and Peru. He had been hired to build a navy for the new empire.

Dundonald describes the poor state of the Brazilian squadron, quarrels over pay and command, the blockade of Bahia, and the politics of Emperor Pedro's court. He also recounts the arrest and exile of the Andrada brothers. The memoir is self-justifying but detailed, a sailor's view of independence wars fought as much in council rooms as at sea.
14914-narrative-of-services-in-the-liber:
Thomas, Earl of Dundonald, admiral of the Red, narrates his services in the liberation of Chile, Peru and Brazil from Spanish and Portuguese domination, in volume one published in London in 1859. Dedicated to the Marquis of Lansdowne, the book claims the public has not yet been placed in a position to judge these events correctly.

Dundonald seeks to discharge a double debt: to set the record straight and to honour those who served. Naval campaigns, sieges and political struggles fill later chapters, from the eighth onward in the contents. The memoir is a sailor's history, partisan and vivid, written by a man who fought the wars he describes and wanted his part known.
19553-the-private-diary-of-dr-john-dee-a:
This volume prints the private diary of Dr. John Dee, the Elizabethan scholar, with a catalog of his great library. Diary entries, with some words in Greek script shown in code, record his daily life, studies, and dealings at court.

The catalog lists works on alchemy, herbs, stars, and the philosopher's stone, from Raymond Lull to Albertus Magnus. Together diary and catalog give a rare view of a Renaissance magus at work, and of the books that fed his learning. A January entry records a tempestuous windy night, and a later one has officials sealing up Mr Webb's chest.
19990-little-abe-or-the-bishop-of-berry-:
Little Abe tells the life of Abraham Lockwood, called the Bishop of Berry Brow. Berry Brow is a Yorkshire village of no pretensions to importance. Its only public building is a Mechanics' Institute of moderate size. One main street, substantially built, holds its life together. From these modest facts rises a local Methodist saint. F. Jewell wrote the life for the Methodist New Connexion. Small places made such bishops in that world.

Lockwood was a working preacher whose parish was one village. His monument is a life, not a building. Jewell's biography records sermons, conversions, and visitations in detail. It shows Wesleyan religion at its most local. Readers meet Victorian faith far below the famous pulpits. Little Abe's fame never left Yorkshire, which is the point.
29895-criminal-man-according-to-the-clas:
Cesare Lombroso's Criminal Man appears here as number 27 of the Science Series, edited by Edward Lee Thorndike and F. E. Beddard. The series ranged widely, from Haddon's Study of Man and Mivart's Groundwork of Science to Geikie's Earth Sculpture, Newcomb's Stars, and Sternberg's Infection and Immunity. Lombroso's volume brings that scientific temper to crime.

The book sets out Lombroso's classification of the criminal man, the system that made his name in criminology. Chapters treat the types, marks, and kinds of criminal character as he ordered them. Read now, the work is both a document of early criminal science and a warning about its limits. It shows how a bold theory tried to sort human wrongdoing into fixed, readable kinds.
33000-a-new-history-of-the-united-states:
Charles Morris's New History of the United States traces the country from its earliest days of discovery and settlement to the eventful year of publication. It is subtitled The Greater Republic and was published in 1899. It shows how thirteen scattered colonies along the Atlantic coast grew into a republic of forty-five states with seventy-five million people and colonial possessions in two hemispheres. More than three hundred engravings illustrate the narrative.

Morris writes as a popular historian, aiming to inspire as well as inform, and his chapters move from exploration and founding through war, expansion, and industry. The book's pride in American growth is plain, and modern readers will read it as a document of its own time as much as a history. As an introduction to the national story as it was told at the century's end, it is vivid and richly pictured.
33750-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, volume four, runs from Bradford, William, to Brequigny, Louis, in the great dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information. Articles listed include three William Bradfords, governor, printer, painter, the cities of Bradford in England and Pennsylvania, Bradford clay, Bradford-on-Avon, Charles Bradlaugh, George Granville Bradley, William de Braose, and Jacques Raymond Brascassat. Articles listed also include Bras d'Or, Pierre Brasdor, and Brasidas.

Further entries cover brass from Nigeria and brass as an alloy, monumental brasses, and Brasseur de Bourbourg. The slice shows the Britannica's range at its Edwardian height: biography, geography, antiquity, and industry side by side, with careful cross-reference and dense, authoritative prose. Researchers will find it a window onto what the English-speaking world knew, and valued, in 1910.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HuieWilliamBrad: An excerpt preserves the prologue of He Slew the Dreamer, William Bradford Huie's book on the killing of Martin Luther King Jr. The identification of the excerpt is marked probable in the record rather than certain. Huie wrote narrative accounts of famous crimes, and his King book followed the hunt for the killer. The entry stands as the opening pages of that work.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JohnsonLyndonBa: Hale Boggs, the Louisiana congressman who served on the Warren Commission, made a gift of a personal statement to the Lyndon Baines Johnson Library. A personal statement given to a presidential library is a participant's deposit for future historians. The surviving record gives the donor and the gift but no text or date, so the entry stands as Boggs's statement placed in Johnson's archive.
narrative-of-services-in-the-liberation-:
Thomas Cochrane, Earl of Dundonald, tells of freeing South America by sea. This second volume, dated 1859, turns to Brazil's war. Don Pedro was proclaimed Emperor of Brazil in its first chapter. Brazil then sought foreign officers and seamen in haste.

The naval command was offered to Cochrane, and he accepted. At Rio he found poor ships and worse crews. Officials tried to cut the pay they had promised him. He refused a sham commission and forced fair terms. Then he blockaded Bahia and rigged fireships that scared the Portuguese fleet. Cochrane's own tale is bold, proud, and full of fight.
nasa-tm-19650015948-preliminary-operatio:
William R Kerslake at Lewis Research Center reported early test results in June 1965 for a new kind of cathode. The device is a wire brush coated with a thick oxide film. It was tried inside electron-bombardment ion thrustors, early electric engines for spacecraft. The summary says the first results pointed to longer thrustor life.

Cathode life limits how long an ion engine can run. A brush form gives a large working surface in a small space. Kerslake presents the operation as preliminary, not final proof. Even so, longer life was a key goal for engines meant to fire gently for months in space.
the-pony-rider-boys-in-the-grand-canyon-:
Frank Gee Patchin's The Pony Rider Boys in the Grand Canyon, or The Mystery of Bright Angel Gulch, lists twenty-four chapters before the story starts. Titles promise a night in the crater and an escape wholly cut off. They promise a battle with the roaring Colorado, dogs picking up a trail, and a new way to hunt lions. The home of the Havasupais appears, and Stacy as an Indian fighter.

Chapter I, Westward Ho!, opens at home rather than in the canyon. Tad Butler is chopping wood behind the woodshed. He finishes a tough, knotted stick before he looks up at the chorus of yells behind him. Three brown-faced young men, his companions of earlier rides, are regarding him solemnly. Patchin begins each series volume with the boys together and the road ahead. The chapter list makes clear that the canyon itself will supply the dangers this time.
the-private-diary-of-dr-john-dee-and-the: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee and the Catalogue of His Library of Manuscripts were printed for the Camden Society from the originals in the Ashmolean Museum and Trinity College, Cambridge. James Orchard Halliwell edited the volume. A transcriber's note explains that Dee's Greek-script English is shown in Rotate-13 code, and diary footnotes take small letters while catalogue notes are numbered. The pages provided hold that note and the title page; the diary entries themselves are not among them.
